extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy, ethicists, and readers interested in Aristotelian accounts of virtue, knowledge, and practical reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: An exposition of Aristotelian distinctions among intellectual and moral faculties (Sense, Intellect, Appetition) and the corresponding excellences (Knowledge, Art, Practical Wisdom, Science, Intuition, Judiciousness) useful for modeling character, deliberation, and moral choice. The text gives definitions, boundaries, and relations among these faculties and shows how they bear on right action and moral development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence as best state relative to function
rubrics_metrics.description: We must discover which is the best state of each of these, because that will be the Excellence of each; and this again is relative to the work each has to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excellence (arete) of a faculty is defined by the best condition of that faculty with respect to the specific function or work it performs. To evaluate a faculty for character-building, ask: what is its proper work, and what state best fulfills that work?

rubrics_metrics.name: Three functions of the soul and moral origination
rubrics_metrics.description: There are in the Soul three functions on which depend moral action and truth; Sense, Intellect, Appetition (vague Desire or definite Will). Sense is the originating cause of no moral action, as brutes have Sense but are in no way partakers of moral action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling moral agency, separate sensory input from intellectual and appetitive faculties; moral responsibility and choice attach to intellect and will, not mere sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Virtue requires true Reason and right Will
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Virtue is a State apt to exercise Moral Choice and Moral Choice is Will consequent on deliberation, so the Reason must be true and the Will right, to constitute good Moral Choice, and what the Reason affirms the Will must pursue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A morally excellent character combines correct belief/reasoning about ends and the correct motivational orientation to pursue what reason affirms. Both cognitive correctness and volitional alignment are required for praiseworthy moral choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation only about the future/contingent
rubrics_metrics.description: No one ever deliberates about things which cannot be otherwise than they are; nothing which is done and past can be the object of Moral Choice; deliberation concerns the future and what may be influenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberative scenes or narrative decisions should focus on contingent matters within an agent's power. Avoid treating past fixed events as objects of genuine deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge (epistēmē): demonstrative, necessary, teachable
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is 'a state or mental faculty apt to demonstrate syllogistically' — what we strictly know cannot be otherwise than it is; Knowledge concerns necessary and eternal things and is capable of being taught via syllogism and induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syllogistic demonstration and appeal to necessary principles when attributing scientific or demonstrative knowledge to a character. Knowledge presupposes that the learner already knows the principles used for teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art (technē): a state conjoined with true Reason apt to make
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is 'a certain state of mind, conjoined with true Reason, apt to Make.' All Art has to do with production and contrivance, concerned with contingent matter that can be made and originates with the maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art/skill in a character should be represented as productive know-how directed at making things (crafts, works), distinct from action aimed at ends in themselves. Art applies where the maker originates the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom (phronēsis): true state conjoined with Reason, apt to do, object human good
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom is 'a state conjoined with reason, true, having human good for its object, and apt to do.' It enables good deliberation about what is expedient for living well and concerns contingent matters of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray practical wisdom as a deliberative faculty that discerns ends and means in human life, grounded in both true reason and concern for human goods. It is neither pure theoretical knowledge nor mere technical craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom requires particulars and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom is not merely knowledge of general principles; one should also know particular details because action is concerned with particulars; experience and age contribute to Practical Wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When showing a character as practically wise, emphasize experience-derived judgment about particulars and context-sensitive know-how rather than only abstract principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition (nous) as grasp of first principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty which takes in the first principles of that which comes under the range of Knowledge cannot be Knowledge, Art, or Practical Wisdom; this last, namely Intuition, performs this function — it takes in first principles and undemonstrable starting points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute to certain characters an intuitive grasp of axiomatic starting points or first principles that cannot themselves be proved; this explains how they can ground demonstrative reasoning or practical judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science (scientia) as union of Knowledge and Intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is the union of Knowledge and Intuition; the Scientific man must not merely know deductions from first principles but be in possession of truth respecting the First Principles — 'Knowledge of the most precious things, with a head on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific excellence combines demonstrative reasoning with grasp of first principles. Use this to distinguish theoreticians (who comprehend principles) from merely skilled practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Counsel (eu boulēma) as rightness of deliberation toward an End
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Counsel is 'Rightness in respect of what conduces to a given End, of which Practical Wisdom is the true conception.' It is not Knowledge, Opinion, or Happy Conjecture; it requires proper end, means, and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent counsels or plans as 'good' only when deliberation aims at proper ends and pursues them by right means at the right time; distinguish good counsel from mere cleverness or lucky hits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciousness (syniēsis/gnōmē) as capacity to judge particulars well
rubrics_metrics.description: Judiciousness is the faculty by virtue of which we call men Judicious; it shares object-matter with Practical Wisdom but differs because it decides upon suggestions and employs the opinionative faculty to judge well when another enunciates matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict judicious characters as those who can take counsel, weigh presented options, and make equitable decisions on particulars without necessarily being the originators (legislators) of policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gnōmē (right judgment/equitable judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty called γνώμη is 'the right judgment of the equitable man.' It tends to make allowance; συγγνώμη (allowance) is right γνώμη having a capacity of making equitable decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gnōmē to characterize moral sensibility that allows for equity and mitigation in judgments — an aspect of practical moral judgment distinct from cold calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Intuition and experience as sources of undemonstrable judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Intuition takes in the extremes at both ends (first and last terms) not by reasoning but by Intuition; these are thought to be gifts of nature and grounded in experience; one should attend to undemonstrable dicta and opinions of the skilful, the old and the Practically-Wise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling elders or experienced advisers, grant them a form of non-syllogistic, experience-based insight that guides judgment and cannot be fully captured by formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleverness (deinotēs) distinct from Practical Wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a faculty commonly named Cleverness, able to do and attain whatever conduces to any given purpose; if that purpose be good the faculty is praiseworthy; Practical Wisdom is not identical with Cleverness though it includes the power to adapt means to ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate characters who are merely clever (effective at means) from those who are practically wise (choose proper ends). Cleverness without goodness can lead to morally wrong outcomes despite technical success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue implies possession of Right Reason (Practical Wisdom); natural vs matured virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is described as a state 'which is accordant with Right Reason'; 'right' means in accordance with Practical Wisdom. Natural Virtue (dispositions present by nature) becomes fully Virtue only when combined with the intellectual element (Practical Wisdom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A morally complete character combines innate dispositions with cultivated practical reasoning; portray moral maturation as the integration of natural tendencies with deliberative insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art admits degrees; Practical Wisdom does not
rubrics_metrics.description: Art admits of degrees of excellence, but Practical Wisdom does not: in Art one who goes wrong purposely may be preferable to him who does so unwittingly, but not so in respect of Practical Wisdom or the other Virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When grading skill versus moral character in narratives, treat technical skill as gradable and improvable, whereas moral wisdom and virtue are presented as qualitative states not merely matters of degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching and method: syllogism and induction
rubrics_metrics.description: All teaching and intellectual learning proceeds on the basis of previous knowledge; there are two ways of teaching, by Syllogism and by Induction. Induction is the source of universal propositions, and Syllogism reasons from these universals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent pedagogical processes as building from particulars (induction) to universals and then using syllogistic reasoning to teach demonstrations; knowledge transmission presumes prior acquaintance with principles.
